lines.text: You've seen that the single owner decides who destroys a value.
Now: exactly when that happens, in what order, and why Rust still lets you skip it.
Here is a pipeline stage. It reads a flag under a reader-writer lock, and if the flag isn't set, it takes the exclusive lock and sets it.
It's the Rust Edition Guide's own example.
Compiled with the two thousand and twenty-one edition, it deadlocks. Here, it hangs forever. Compiled with the two thousand and twenty-four edition, it runs.
Same source. The only thing that changed is when a temporary dies.
First what a destructor is and where it runs. Then when a temporary dies, which is what changed.
By the end, you'll place every destructor in a program on a timeline, build a wrapper that closes a file exactly once, and know why leaking is allowed.
When a value is no longer needed, Rust runs its destructor.
And a destructor is two parts.
First, your drop, if the type has one. Then the compiler's own drop glue, which drops every field... in the order you wrote them.
So this stage logs its own name first, then name, input, and the spill file, which we build in a few steps.
Most types never write a drop at all. The glue already drops their fields.
Our probe, a trace... is just a value whose drop writes its name to a log.
Let's predict one.
Three locals are declared one after another: first a, then b, then c.
At the closing brace... in what order do they die?
The reverse. C, then b, then a.
That's the opposite of struct fields. It's the stack discipline, and it keeps a later value that borrows an earlier one sound... the guard dies before what it points at.
Where does a value die? Where its last owner ends.
After a move, the owner is the new binding.
So the value dies there.
At the closing brace.
The brace in main... drops nothing for it, because nothing is left there.
The standard drop function isn't magic. It takes ownership and returns, so the value dies right there.
And overwriting a variable builds the new value first, then drops the old one.

lines.text: Say your type implements drop. You hold a value, and you call its drop method directly.
Does the compiler let you run the destructor by hand?
Rejected. The compiler gives the explicit destructor call error.
Your call would run drop, and then the brace would run it again... so Rust forbids the call, and offers the standard drop function instead.
Why is a file handle... not allowed to be copied?
Because two copies would close the same file twice.
A type with a drop manages something besides its own bytes, so a bitwise copy would duplicate that responsibility.
That's why copy and drop never meet. The compiler rejects it.
Put three rules together. One owner. A move empties the source. And no copy on a type with a destructor.
Never twice isn't a convention... it's a theorem. Exactly once follows whenever the drop code runs at all. And Rust doesn't promise that.
Now the real thing. A spill file is a temporary file that gets closed and deleted in its drop.
So in Rust, this pattern is simply ownership plus drop.
Hand it through two functions and back... one close, one unlink.
No defer. No finally. No with. There is exactly one owner, and its scope end is the release.
The file itself is four bytes, the descriptor.
One caveat: errors on close are ignored by drop. Call sync all first, if they matter.
A spool owns a directory guard and a file guard, in that order.
The directory's drop removes the directory. The file's drop removes the file.
After the spool is dropped, what's left on disk?
The directory stays.
The directory guard is declared first, so it drops first, while the file is still inside... and removing a full directory fails.
Declare the spill file first, and both go.
A temporary is a value with no name.
It ends at the semicolon. That lock is released before the next statement.
Unless a let borrows it... then it lives to the end of the block.
And a match keeps its temporaries alive through every arm.
That's how a lock gets held longer than it looks.
Back to the stage under the old edition. The migration lint fires.
You run the automatic fix.
What does it produce... and is the deadlock gone?
It rewrites the condition into a match... and the match keeps the old order. The deadlock stays.
The guide says: review each rewrite, and put the if let back where you want the shorter life.
Rust two thousand and twenty-four changes two temporary scopes. Both make a temporary die sooner.
In two thousand and twenty-four, a temporary made in the condition is gone before the else branch.
In a block's tail expression, they drop before the block's own locals.
That one badge, landing on the other side of the else, is the whole difference between hanging and running.
A match is unchanged.

lines.text: The Rust two thousand and twenty-four migration guide shows another example. A function ends with a borrow of a ref cell, as its tail expression.
Which editions compile it?
Only the two thousand and twenty-four edition.
In the old edition, the borrow guard outlived the cell itself, so the compiler refused... the does-not-live-long-enough error.
Now the guard goes first, and it compiles.
Here's a value moved on one path only.
So at the closing brace, who knows whether to drop it?
Only the running program does. So the compiler keeps a hidden boolean flag, and checks it at the brace.
You can see it in the compiler's intermediate code: a constant true, a constant false, and a switch.
Destructors run on the normal path. And a panic still drops everything on its way out, in the same reverse order.
But process exit drops nothing.
And with panic set to abort, nothing either.
So a spill file is cleaned up after a panic, but not after an exit. And when main returns, every other thread dies where it stands, destructors unrun.
One more rule. If a drop panics while already unwinding, the whole process aborts. Keep drop bodies simple.
Mem forget takes a value and never drops it.
The file stays open, and on disk. The path's buffer is never freed... the counting allocator sees one allocation too many.
And all of that is safe code.
Because Rust never promised destructors would run.
Leaking is usually a bug. But it's a memory-safe bug.

lines.text: Four ways... to end up with a value that never drops.
Which of the first three needs unsafe? Or none?
None of them. Leaking is safe... forget, box leak, a reference-count cycle, process exit.
The unsafe one is running a destructor by hand, with manually drop's drop, because nothing stops it running twice.
Two honest ways to skip a destructor, on purpose.
Manually drop holds the same data, with no automatic drop. Take the value back out, and it drops again.
Box leak: cut the owner, keep the bytes for the whole program.
Neither one fixes drop order. For that, reorder your declarations.

lines.text: That was just before the first stable release of Rust.
Long ago, a thread API gave out a guard whose drop joined the child thread. The child borrowed the parent's stack, so the parent couldn't leave first.
Then someone forgot the guard, in safe code.
The parent's frame went away, and the child kept running, with a reference into it.
Safe code. And still unsound.
The fix wasn't to forbid leaks. It was to admit that destructors may never run.
So put the guarantee in a function call, not in a destructor.
A scoped thread block joins every thread before it returns. A return can't be forgotten.
The general rule: unsafe code must never rely on drop running.

And when you hand out a proxy, make the owner safe first. The vector sets its length to the start of the drained range before it gives out a drain, zero for a full drain. Forget the drain, and you only leak more.
Leaking one value can leak much more, and that is called leak amplification.
Prove it, one of three.
A function takes a parameter a, a tuple parameter with b and c, and has one local, d.
So, in what order do the four values drop?
D, c, b, a.
The local first. Then the parameters, last and in reverse... and inside the tuple pattern, c before b.
Two of three.
You write let underscore equals a lock on the shared value, and then increment a counter.
Is the counter protected?
The compiler refuses it.
An underscore binds nothing, so the guard would be gone by the end of that statement... and the increment would run unlocked. That is exactly why that line is a lint.
Name the guard.
Three of three. A code review.
Someone proposes an API with a guard. The guard must be dropped, or the device keeps writing into the buffer.
Is it sound?

lines.text: Unsound. A safe caller can forget the guard, the buffer is freed, and the device keeps writing.
Soundness may never depend on drop running.
Move the stop into a function that takes a closure, like thread scope.

lines.text: Six things to keep.
A destructor is your drop, then the fields, in order. Locals go in reverse.
A temporary is gone at its semicolon... and the two thousand and twenty-four edition ends two of them sooner.
One owner means exactly one release, never two.
Leaking is safe. So soundness never depends on drop running.
A type with a drop... keeps its fields until it dies.
